criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1: Rather than examining household or community water or sanitation service access, this paper assesses the technical pollutant-removal performance, social acceptability, and prospective regulatory feasibility of deploying a Nature-based Solution (constructed wetland / 'Biojardinera') prototype for on-site greywater effluent treatment to reduce river water pollution (explicitly framed around SDG 6.3 water-quality and wastewater-treatment targets). In the Real-World Lab neighborhood, households already have municipal piped water and domestic plumbing/septic tanks, and baseline 100% greywater discharge to stormwater gutters is described only as background context motivating the green-infrastructure prototype.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper PASSES because Sections 2.3, 3.2.1, 3.3, and 4.3 explicitly analyze regulatory, legal, and institutional factors in Costa Rica (fragmented institutional competencies among AyA, municipalities, ASADAS, MINAE, and Ministry of Health; municipal water tariffs covering only drinking water and stormwater; rare enforcement of General Health Law No. 5395 against gutter greywater discharge; construction permits and 1-meter property-line setbacks under Decree 39887-S-MINAE; effluent discharge limits and reuse rules under Decree 33601-MINAE-S; and multi-agency regulations governing public space). However, under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, the paper FAILS C2 because the regulations analyzed in the focus groups govern environmental and construction permitting for building NbS greywater biofilter prototypes and discharging treated effluent—not household eligibility, connection, tariff affordability, disconnection, or access to water/sanitation services—while municipal water-tax scope and non-enforcement are discussed only as unanalysed status-quo background. Note that even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, overall full-text eligibility remains 'exclude' because C1 and C4 fail.
criterion_notes.c3: Passes C3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical data, including 10 water-quality sampling campaigns across 3 points of an operational constructed-wetland prototype, a structured survey of 154 residents, open interviews with 5 municipal officials, semi-structured interviews with 7 water-sector experts, participatory field observations/mapping, and focus groups with 13 water-management experts.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4: Reported empirical outcomes are (1) effluent pollutant concentrations and removal efficiencies (%) at an office-building wetland prototype (plus 10 literature wetlands), (2) resident liking of greywater-irrigated plants (77%), ornamental plant preference (88% Heliconia), and hypothetical monthly willingness-to-pay (mean US$7.4/month) for greywater treatment, and (3) expert subjective ratings ('Low' in public space vs. 'High' on private land) of 4-10 year NbS prototype implementation probability. None of these measure household/community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, realized affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Passes C5: The transdisciplinary Real-World Lab mixed-methods case study design, study sites in Costa Rica, samples/units of analysis for each empirical component, regulatory/contextual factors discussed, and technical/attitudinal/feasibility outcomes are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Passes C6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study assesses the technical, socio-economic, and political-regulatory dimensions relevant to implementing NbS for decentralized greywater treatment.

Progress towards achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 6 is advancing very slowly in the region, particularly for SDG 6.3, which aims to improve water quality, wastewater treatment, and safe reuse [22].

The purpose was to evaluate the regulatory feasibility of implementing this type of decentralized greywater treatment infrastructure in Costa Rica. Thirteen experts from various water-related institutions were interviewed

For the municipalities, the taxation of water prices covers only for the supply of drinking water and stormwater management. Therefore, the provision of a centralized wastewater infrastructure does not seem economically feasible.

Discharge to a receiving water body requires obtaining a permit from the Ministry of Health, which mandates monitoring and control of the effluent to ensure that specific water quality parameters are met.
The survey aimed to gather insights into social preferences, acceptability, receptiveness, willingness, economic disposition, and capacity to implement NbS for decentralized greywater treatment.

In our survey, we sought to determine the willingness and ability of homeowners to pay for a treatment service, an expense that does not exist in the current situation. Citizens reported willingness to pay an average of US-$ 7.4 monthly for this service.

raw_response.exposure: Technical, socio-economic, and political-regulatory conditions for implementing decentralized greywater treatment Nature-based Solutions (Biojardineras), including public-space versus private-property siting and permitting/setback/effluent-discharge regulations (Decrees 39887-S-MINAE and 33601-MINAE-S, General Health Law No. 5395)
raw_response.outcome: Prototype greywater pollutant concentrations and removal efficiencies (COD, solids, nutrients, fats, surfactants/MBAS, fecal coliforms, E. coli); resident acceptability (77%), ornamental plant preference (88%), and hypothetical willingness-to-pay (mean US$7.4/month); and expert qualitative ratings ('Low' in public space vs. 'High' on private property) of 4-10 year NbS prototype implementation likelihood
raw_response.population_and_sample: 1 operational horizontal subsurface flow constructed wetland ('Biojardinera') prototype at CNFL Sustainability Farm in Coronado (10 water-quality sampling rounds across 3 points) plus 10 literature Biojardineras; 154 surveyed households/properties in the Real-World Lab neighborhood (Llorente district, Canton of Flores, Great Metropolitan Area); 5 municipal environmental officials, 7 water-sector experts (semi-structured interviews), and 13 water-management experts in focus groups
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; also fails C2 under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading and C4 on outcomes). This transdisciplinary Real-World Lab study in Costa Rica evaluates the technical pollutant-removal performance, resident aesthetic acceptance and hypothetical willingness-to-pay, and prospective regulatory permitting feasibility of a Nature-based Solution prototype (horizontal subsurface flow constructed wetland, 'Biojardinera') for decentralized greywater effluent treatment to reduce river water pollution (SDG 6.3). It does not examine household or community access to water or sanitation services (C1), its regulatory analysis concerns construction/environmental discharge permitting for NbS biofilter prototypes rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access (C2 narrow), and its empirical outcomes are office-prototype pollutant removal efficiencies, resident plant/concept preferences and hypothetical WTP, and expert ratings of 4-10 year technology implementation probability rather than service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (C4). Even under the plain broad reading of Criterion 2 (where the regulatory feasibility analysis passes C2), the study remains excluded because C1 and C4 are not met.
raw_response.study_design: Transdisciplinary mixed-methods case study (Real-World Lab combining NbS prototype water-quality sampling, literature synthesis of 10 constructed wetlands, stakeholder/municipal interviews, field observations, structured resident survey, and expert focus groups)
